questions.enonce_markdown:
Define the following terms as used in genetics:

(i) Allele
(ii) Codominance
(iii) Phenotype
(iv) Mutation. *(2, 2, 2 marks)*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) An **allele** is one of the alternative forms of a gene, found at the same position (locus) on homologous chromosomes. *Example:* the alleles $\mathrm{Hb^A}$ and $\mathrm{Hb^S}$ of the haemoglobin gene.

(ii) **Codominance** is the situation in which both alleles of a gene are fully expressed in the heterozygote, neither being dominant over the other. *Example:* blood group AB ($I^A I^B$).

(iii) **Phenotype** is the observable (physical or physiological) characteristic of an organism, resulting from its genotype and the influence of the environment. *Example:* tall, blood group O.

(iv) A **mutation** is a sudden, random change in the structure or amount of the genetic material (a gene or a chromosome). *Example:* the change in one base of the haemoglobin gene that causes sickle-cell anaemia.

questions.enonce_markdown: Sickle-cell anaemia is a genetic disorder caused by a recessive allele. The allele for normal haemoglobin production is $\mathrm{Hb^A}$ while that for sickle-cell anaemia is $\mathrm{Hb^S}$. Using suitable symbols and diagrams determine the genotypes, phenotypes and probabilities of the offspring for a cross between two parents having the sickle-cell trait (heterozygous). *(10 marks)*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Key:** $\mathrm{Hb^A}$ = allele for normal haemoglobin; $\mathrm{Hb^S}$ = allele for sickle-cell haemoglobin (recessive).

**Parents:** both heterozygous, genotype $\mathrm{Hb^A Hb^S}$ (sickle-cell trait carriers, who are healthy or only mildly affected).

**Parents' genotypes:** $\mathrm{Hb^A Hb^S}$ $\times$ $\mathrm{Hb^A Hb^S}$

**Gametes (after meiosis):** $\mathrm{Hb^A}$ or $\mathrm{Hb^S}$ from each parent

**Punnett square:**

| Gametes | $\mathrm{Hb^A}$ | $\mathrm{Hb^S}$ |
|---|---|---|
| **$\mathrm{Hb^A}$** | $\mathrm{Hb^A Hb^A}$ | $\mathrm{Hb^A Hb^S}$ |
| **$\mathrm{Hb^S}$** | $\mathrm{Hb^A Hb^S}$ | $\mathrm{Hb^S Hb^S}$ |

**Offspring (F1):**

| Genotype | Phenotype | Probability |
|---|---|---|
| $\mathrm{Hb^A Hb^A}$ | Normal (homozygous normal) | 1/4 (25 %) |
| $\mathrm{Hb^A Hb^S}$ | Normal but carrier: sickle-cell trait | 2/4 = 1/2 (50 %) |
| $\mathrm{Hb^S Hb^S}$ | Sickle-cell anaemia (sickler) | 1/4 (25 %) |

**Genotypic ratio** 1 $\mathrm{Hb^A Hb^A}$ : 2 $\mathrm{Hb^A Hb^S}$ : 1 $\mathrm{Hb^S Hb^S}$. **Phenotypic ratio** 3 healthy (1 normal : 2 carriers) : 1 sickle-cell anaemia, so each child has a **25 % chance** of having sickle-cell anaemia, a 75 % chance of not having the disease, and a 50 % chance of being a carrier.

questions.enonce_markdown: Why are people with sickle-cell anaemia (sicklers) more resistant to malaria than persons with normal haemoglobin? *(2 marks)*
questions.corrige_markdown:
The malaria parasite (*Plasmodium*) lives and multiplies inside the **red blood cells**. In people with the sickle-cell allele, the abnormal haemoglobin makes the red cells **sickle-shaped and fragile**. When the cell is infected, it collapses or is quickly destroyed (removed by the spleen), so the parasite **cannot complete its development** and the number of parasites stays low. These people therefore suffer less from malaria than people with normal haemoglobin.

*Note:* carriers ($\mathrm{Hb^A Hb^S}$) have the best advantage in malaria regions, because they are protected against malaria without suffering the severe anaemia of $\mathrm{Hb^S Hb^S}$.
